newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIAN BROADCASTING CORP MIDDAY UPDATE.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIAN BROADCASTING CORP MIDDAY UPDATE.

text.p: THREDBO RESCUE WRAPS UP AS NATION PULLS TOGETHER
In the Snowy Mountains, preparations are being made to transport the last of the bodies recovered from the Thredbo landslide to Sydney.
The landslide last week caused the collapse of two ski lodges at the New South Wales ski resort of Thredbo.
Formal identification is to be completed and post mortem examinations undertaken in preparation for the Coroner's inquest into the tragedy, which has claimed 18 lives.

Meanwhile, New South Wales State Emergency Services executive director Horrie Howard said he will ask the State Government about the possibility of a special fund for volunteers "out of pocket" because of their efforts at Thredbo.
Some volunteers in the resuce operation have expressed concern their employers will dock their pay.
Mr Howard said the idea of a special fund is worth looking at, together with any other initiatives that can protect volunteers who lose pay.
And a Queensland business is challenging others to donate money for the volunteers.
Cheryl McAlonan from IBS Engineering in Innisfail said her company will donate the wage of one volunteer and wants other companies to follow suit.
"These people have been going through a lot of stress and strain and these people are all volunteers and have been doing a fabulous job and we'd like to let them know," she said.
"We are all Australians, and we are pulling together and we'd like to do our part as well."
But one of New South Wales' big rescue organisations has said it would be surprised if any of its members lost pay while away from work for the rescue.
Greg Miller, from the state's Volunteer Rescue Association, saidsquad members have to be available immediately in emergencies and most had arrangements in place with their employers.
PROFESSOR SAYS SAUDI ARABIA NOT BOUND BY AUSTRALIAN COURT ORDERS
An Adelaide law professor says the Government in Saudi Arabia will not necessarily be bound by any order issued by the South Australian Supreme Court to stop any execution of two British nurses.
They are accused of murdering South Australian nurse, Yvonne Gilford.
The two are launching legal action in the Supreme Court to stop their possible execution, if they are found guilty.
Associate Professor of Law at the University of South Australia, Rick Sarre said the situation is similar to the Melbourne case involving the Gillespie children.
He said in that case, the Family Court in Australia made a very specific order that the Gillespie children, who had been kidnapped from Melbourne, should be returned from Malaysia.
"The Malaysian court said, or the Malaysian authorities said: 'that's all well and good for you to say', but they are still there," he said.
So in many respects, this area of private international law, particularly a muddy and murky one, is one that relies I think more on politics than it does on law."
MAN APPEARS OVER DEATH OF MUSICAL DIRECTOR IN MELBOURNE
In Melbourne, a 29-year-old youth worker has appeared in the County Court over an accident last year, in which Sunset Boulevard musical director Brian Stacey was killed.
Simon Andrew Lenton of Parkville has pleaded guilty to failing to stop after an accident, failing to report an accident and careless driving.
The court was told that in the early hours of October 25 last year Mr Lenton's car struck Mr Stacey's motorcycle at the intersection of Rathdowne and Elgin streets in Carlton.
Mr Stacey was thrown against a post and died from internal injuries.
The court heard Mr Lenton left the scene of the accident but later admitted to the Legal Aid Commission that he was the driver.
The case is continuing.
FISCHER SAYS BARNARD WAS "A GREAT AUSTRALIAN"
Acting Prime Minister Tim Fischer says Lance Barnard was a great Australian and Tasmanian, who made a significant contribution to the nation, Launceston, and the Labor Party.
The former Deputy Prime Minister died yesterday in Melbourne.
Mr Fischer said he always found Mr Barnard a kindly man, who will have a place in history as Minister for a record number of portfolios at the start of the Whitlam Government in 1972.
PROPOSAL TO ALLOW SAFARI HUNTING OF CROCODILES IN TOP END
A proposal to allow safari hunting of crocodiles in Arnhem land is among submissions to a Senate inquiry into farming native wildlife, which held public hearings in the Northern Territory this week.
The Senate comittee has completed hearings in the Territory and is now heading to Perth.
The region's Ramingining Murwangi Station already has a small scale buffalo safari hunting operation and a successful Crocodile Hatchery.
It wants to be able to offer up to four large male crocodiles per year to hunters who are willing to pay for such a trophy.
The Senate committee has received 330 submissions nationally.
Most Northern Territory submissions have been dominated by issues relating to the Crocodile industry.
There were also calls to develop a harvesting and export industry for the red-tailed black cockatoo.

In its submission the Northern Land Council called a number of national and regional workshops on commercial use of native wildlife and assistance to Land councils to develop policies. -- Reuters Sydney 61-2 9373-1800
